Q: How do you show the action buttons in an editor header A:

  1. Open Settings

  2. Search for debug toolbar

  3. Look for "Debug Tool Bar Location"

  4. Change it from "hidden" or "floating" to "docked"

Alternatively, search for these specific settings:

  • debug.toolBarLocation - Set to docked to show buttons in the editor header

  • debug.showInStatusBar - to "always" or "onFirstSessionStart"

Q: select random rows from the dataframe A:

There is a concept of a "sample" in Spark that lets us take a random sample of a df.
Refer to this link: spark sample.

A quick exsmple:

Let’s say final_df is your merged / joined df.

random_df = final_df.sample(0.1).show()  # here 0.1 says 10% of records to show / include in random_df

Q: Feeling stuck after 2–3 years of C++ — normal learning curve or wrong approach? A:

The amount useful comments on this particular question is heart warming. I can see some progress regarding the attitude and attention towards learning C++.

I will start with the last paragraph of the OP: It's actually fortunate of you to not have much experience with C. Basic familiarity with C becomes a blockade of stamina for all but the nerdiest weirdos among us. Knowing other languages is generally good, but IMO " C++ first, C next " is a more smooth path to learning C++.

C++ is a complicated language with an endless appetite to absorb newer features. It's natural to be overwhelmed at the beginning. But there's a right path toward learning it. As always ,I suggest you pick a book titled Modern C++, first published not sooner than a decade ago. And my favorite line is: read C++ in reverse historical order of its features; the further we go forward in time, the developer-friendlier C++ becomes. C++23 is stable now, and you can use compiler explorer for self tutoring. In 2 years, C++23 should become the baseline standard version. So, by the time you're ready to market, so is market to you. I won't mention core guidelines again, but it's a must read.

About the philosophy:

  • UB is what phobics mention as C++'s downside. But it's actually the culprit of every engineering tool. There are usage senarios that void every warrantee or guarantee for any tool. C++ standard documents these cases as Undefined behavior, and there's lots of them. Any digital production tool with sufficient complexity, has to document similar scenarios one way or another.

  • Object life-time has been the core of C++ language since day one. Using an object outside it's life-time scope is UB. You need learn about storage class, linkage, and visiblity of identifiers, functions and objects. Then comes Stroustrup's most brilliant discovery: RAII, the distinguishing feature of C++, among classic programming languages. He did find a recurring pattern among all resource management portions of code, and incorporated it into the language. Over the years pioneers cemented this legacy by an idiom called rule 350.

  • pointer avoidance: Unlike C where pointer is the big hammer, in C++ we generally try to push pointers as far away as feasible. C++ has far more tools for abstraction and genericness. You will learn them in time. The primary usage as by-reference parameters has had C++ references as the replacement since day one. Other use case have library utilities in std the standard C++ namespace.

That's enough for starters; I am not writing a book. Just one last tip: std is your best friend. Check for a solution inside that library before anything else.

Q: Excel - Use Scan with multiple input arrays A:

Respectable VBasic2008 made a grave mistake. =LET(values,A2:A11,checks,B2:B11,SCAN(0,values*(values>checks),LAMBDA(a,i,IF(i,i+a,0)))) will fail if the value is zero but greater than check.

Evidently, no number value is suitable for this purpose. Such non-number value like error shall be used instead:

[H1]=SCAN(0,array1/(array1>array2),LAMBDA(a,i,IFERROR(i+a,0)))

Surely, this is the particular solution. DjC and Tom Sharpe provide with general solutions.
